summary: This RFC defines how to implement channel bindings for EAP methods, to address the lying NAS problem and the lying provider problem, in which a network access server or provider misrepresents who it is or what it offers.

plainLanguage.summary: Channel binding lets the server check that the access point told the client the same thing that it told the server. The client passes the access point's own information on to the server over the protected part of the login exchange, and the server compares it with its own records. If they do not match, the server reports a failure.

subtitle: How an EAP client and server catch an access point or visited network that lies about what it offers.

tldr.problem: In EAP pass-through mode the access point can tell the client one thing about the network and the AAA server another, so a less trusted network can pose as a more trusted one, and a visited provider can advertise roaming terms that are not true.
tldr.mechanism: After the EAP method has derived keys, the client sends the authenticator's own words to the EAP server inside the protected EAP channel. The server compares them with the AAA attributes it received and with a local database, then returns a success or failure code.
tldr.outcome: The server can detect the inconsistency but cannot say which party is lying, and the mechanism needs updated EAP methods, updated client drivers and a trustworthy database to work at all.

facts.label: Example channel-binding budget
facts.value: 384 octets with EAP-GPSK and a 1020-octet EAP MTU

today: RFC 6677 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says it is only part of a defense: lower layers still have to specify what goes into i1, EAP methods still have to describe how the data is carried, and deployments still have to decide what the local database holds.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6677 defines how to implement channel bindings for Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) methods, in order to address the lying Network Access Server problem and the lying provider problem.

In pass-through mode, a Network Access Server (NAS) may represent one set of information to the backend Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) infrastructure while representing contrary information to EAP peers. The same false information may also be provided to both the peer and the EAP server, and a lying entity can sit anywhere on the AAA path between the NAS and the EAP server.

The mechanism puts information about the characteristics of the service provided by the authenticator into the EAP method, protected within it. The server can then verify that the authenticator is providing information to the peer that is consistent with the information received from that authenticator and with the information stored about it.
sections.plainLanguage: A network access point can tell a client one set of facts and the authentication server another. Channel binding lets the client pass the access point's information on to the server over a protected channel, so the server can compare the two.

sections.title: The Problem the Check Has to Catch
sections.content:
The goal is to make sure that the authenticator provides correct information to the EAP peer during network discovery, selection, and authentication. In an enterprise network with a single administrative domain, the EAP server can hold information about all the authenticators in the network. In a service provider network, global knowledge is infeasible because of roaming, so the goal becomes making sure that the level of service a peer receives is consistent with the contractual agreement between the two providers.

The RFC lists example attacks. A corporate campus with VLANs for a firewalled network and for a public guest network may have access points on both, served by the same EAP server but broadcasting different SSIDs. A compromised access point on the guest network could advertise the SSID of the corporate network, to lure peers into sending confidential information over a weaker connection. A mobile phone provider could advertise very competitive flat rates but send per-minute rates to the home server, or boost its towers' transmission power and advertise the network identity of the neighbouring country's provider, so that handsets roam without realizing it.

Channel bindings detect inconsistencies in the information from a visited network, but cannot determine which entity is lying. They verify only the endpoints; if intermediate hops also need protecting, the AAA protocol in use has to do that.
sections.plainLanguage: The attacks this addresses are about trust: a weak network pretending to be a strong one, or a provider pretending to offer terms it does not offer. The check finds a disagreement between what the client was told and what the server was told. It does not identify who made the false claim.

sections.title: Two Ways to Bind the Channel
sections.content:
EAP channel bindings authenticate information that the authenticator gave the EAP peer without protection. They work by letting the peer and the server compare their two views of the network's properties inside a secure channel. This differs from the channel bindings described in RFC 5056, which bind the endpoints of a multi-layer protocol so that lower layers can protect data from higher layers.

The RFC describes two categories of approach. After keys have been derived, the peer and the server can exchange plaintext information about the network in an integrity-protected channel and check it for consistency. Or the peer and the server can each uniquely encode their own view without exchanging it, producing an opaque blob that is included directly in the derivation of the EAP session keys.

Both approaches apply only to key-deriving EAP methods. Exchanging plaintext allows policy-based comparisons rather than precise matches for every field, which gives a policy-defined consistency instead of bitwise equality. It works with EAP methods that already support extensible integrity-protected channels, and because it does not touch the key derivation it makes debugging, incremental deployment, backward compatibility and a logging mode easier. Deriving the keys directly from the channel information instead supports EAP methods that cannot carry protected data, since the key derivation can be revised or the method wrapped, and it guarantees the channel information, because differences in it would yield different session keys and the session could not continue.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to do this. The client and the server can exchange what they know over the protected part of the login and compare it, or each side can fold its view into the keys it derives, so that a mismatch breaks the session. The first is easier to deploy and to debug.

sections.title: The Channel-Binding Protocol
sections.content:
Channel bindings are always provided between two endpoints, the EAP peer and the EAP server, which communicate through an authenticator. During network advertisement, selection, and authentication, the authenticator presents unauthenticated information to the peer. The RFC calls this message i1. It can include an authenticator identifier and the identity of the network it represents, in addition to advertised network information such as offered services and roaming information, and the type of media in use may be communicated implicitly in it. Because there is no established trust relationship between the peer and the authenticator, the peer has no way to validate this information.

During the transaction the authenticator also presents a number of information properties about itself and the current request, in the form of AAA attributes. The RFC calls this i2. It is the information the AAA server receives from the last hop in the proxy chain, which is not necessarily the authenticator. AAA hops between the authenticator and the AAA server can validate some of i2, but whether the AAA server can rely on that depends on the business relationship with the proxies and on the structure of the AAA network.

A local database makes the check meaningful. It holds trustworthy information about each NAS or authenticator in an enterprise deployment, or about each roaming partner in a service provider deployment, and it can use wildcards, for example a check that all IEEE 802.11 access points on a given subnet use a specific SSID. During an EAP method execution with channel bindings, the peer sends i1 to the EAP server, which checks it for consistency against i2 and against the database. The server then sends the peer a message saying whether the validation succeeded or failed, including the attributes that were used in the check.

If compliance with the authoritative policy source is mandatory and the consistency check failed, the server MUST send an EAP-Failure message to terminate the session after reporting the failure. If the server is configured otherwise, it MUST allow the session to complete normally and leave the decision about network access to the peer's policy. Information that failed to comply with policy MUST NOT be listed among the attributes used for the binding, and the server SHOULD indicate channel-binding failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Three sets of information are compared. What the access point told the client, what the access point told the AAA server, and what the server has stored itself. The server reports success or failure and, if the check is required, ends the login.

sections.title: Message Format, Codes and Namespaces
sections.content:
An EAP method that supports channel binding provides a way to carry channel-binding data from the peer to the EAP server and a channel-binding response back. The specifics of the transport depend on the method, but the content of both messages is defined by the RFC.

Both the data and the response start with a one-byte code, followed by one set of fields for each type of attribute. Each set holds a Length of two octets in network byte order, giving the length of the namespace-specific data and excluding the NSID and length octets; an NSID of one octet, naming the namespace the attributes are drawn from; and the namespace-specific data itself. A given NSID MUST NOT appear more than once in a channel-binding data or a channel-binding response, so all the data for a namespace sits inside one set of fields. The set may be repeated when several namespaces are included.

Three codes are defined. Code 1 marks channel-binding data from the client, and carries the full attributes and values the peer wants the server to validate. Code 2 is a response reporting success, and the server returns the attributes it considered when it decided that the binding was valid; attributes the server cannot check, or that failed to validate, MUST NOT be returned in a success response. Code 3 is a response reporting failure, meaning that server policy found the client's attributes did not accurately describe the authenticator; the server SHOULD include the attributes that did validate, and MAY include no attributes at all.

The RADIUS namespace uses identifier 1. Inside it, RADIUS attribute-value pairs are encoded with a one-octet type, a one-octet length that includes the type and length octets and is at least 3, and the value of the attribute. The full value of an attribute is included in the channel-binding data and response. Namespace identifier 255 is reserved for private use. Peers MUST treat unknown codes as channel-binding failure, MUST ignore attributes contained in a field with an unknown NSID, MUST ignore any attributes in a response that were not present in the channel-binding data, and MUST ignore differences between the attribute values sent and the ones returned.
sections.plainLanguage: The message starts with a number that says whether it carries the client's data, a success, or a failure. After that come one or more groups of attributes, each group marked with a namespace number so the reader knows how to interpret the bytes.

sections.title: System Requirements
sections.content:
The channel-binding protocol must be transported after keying material has been derived between the EAP peer and the server, and before the peer would suffer adverse effects from joining an adversarial network.

The transport protocol MUST support end-to-end message integrity protection between the peer and the server, to prevent an adversarial NAS or AAA device from manipulating the transported data. It SHOULD provide confidentiality, because the channel bindings can contain private information including peer identities. If confidentiality cannot be provided, private information MUST NOT be sent as part of the channel-binding information. The transport also has to stay within the MTU of the lower-layer medium, and methods that exchange the information inside protected EAP channels may not support fragmentation. The RFC gives an example: if the EAP MTU is 1020 octets and EAP Generalized Pre-Shared Key is used with maximal-length identities, at most 384 octets are available for channel-binding information, while methods such as EAP Tunneled Transport Layer Security support fragmentation and could carry significantly longer payloads.

When the data travels directly within an EAP method, the method MUST be able to carry integrity-protected data from the peer to the server and from the server to the peer, MUST exchange channel-binding data with the AAA subsystem hosting the EAP server, and MUST be able to import channel-binding data from the lower layer on the peer. Lower-layer protocols MUST support EAP, and they MUST support EAP methods that derive keying material, since otherwise no integrity-protected channel is available to run the protocol in. They need not support traffic encryption, which is independent of the authentication phase.

A new RADIUS attribute, EAP-Lower-Layer, carries the identity of the lower layer over which EAP is transported. Its type is 163, its length is 6, and its value is a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order taken from the IANA registry of EAP lower layers. It MAY be sent by the NAS to the RADIUS server in an Access-Request or an Accounting-Request packet. Lower layers need enough information in i1 to identify which lower layer is involved, and the preferred way to do that is with this attribute, which MUST be included in i1 unless an attribute specific to a particular lower layer is included instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The check runs over a protected channel, so it needs keys that only the client and the server hold. The data also has to fit inside the packet size of the link below it. A new RADIUS attribute tells the server which kind of link the login is running over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The trust model assumes that the EAP peer and the authentication server are honest, while the authenticator is maliciously sending false information to the peer, to the server, or to both. The server trusts that the channel-binding information it received from the peer is the information the peer received from the authenticator, the peer trusts the channel-binding result received from the server, and the server trusts the information in its local database. To establish the first two of these during an EAP execution, the EAP method MUST provide mutual authentication between peer and server, derivation of keying material that includes an integrity-protection key known to the peer and the EAP server but not the authenticator, and transmission of both the request and the result over integrity-protected channels.

Existing cryptographic binding does not typically provide the mutual authentication that channel binding requires. An authenticator could establish an outer tunnel that terminates at itself, which discloses the Master Session Key of the inner method and typically lets the authenticator attack cryptographic binding. If the authenticator controls the binding, it controls the channel-binding parameters and results, so an authenticator that is supposed to be distinguished from another can claim services it was not authorized to offer.

Dishonest peers can manipulate only the first message, i1. If the altered i1 fails validation, the channel-binding validation fails. If it passes, then either the original i1 was wrong and i1 corrected the problem, or both are valid, and a peer that gains an advantage in auditing or charging this way can be detected by including the information in i2 and checking i1 against i2. A server cannot generally tell whether the authenticator advertised incorrect information or the peer is dishonest, which matters before a validation failure is used to judge the reputation of either one. Dishonest servers can abort any EAP session, and can also claim a successful validation even when i1 holds invalid information; channel binding can neither prevent nor detect that, and such attacks have to be handled by policy.

The RFC also warns about bid-down attacks on the negotiation of channel binding. Many EAP state machines accept a success message at any point after key derivation, and EAP success messages are not integrity protected, so an attacker able to insert a message can generate one, and the NAS is always in a position to do so. Privacy violations are a further concern. Binding the username attribute can confirm an authenticator's guess: a peer may send a privacy-protecting anonymous identifier in its EAP identity message and the full username in the protected i1 message, while the authenticator sends its guess in i2 instead of the anonymous identifier, so a failed check tells the authenticator that the guess was right.
sections.plainLanguage: The method depends on the client and the server trusting each other. It cannot catch an authenticator and a server that lie together, and it cannot stop a network from hiding the fact that it supports channel binding at all. Binding a username can even confirm a guess made by the access point.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
A new top-level registry was created for Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Channel Binding Parameters, made up of several sub-registries. The channel-binding codes sub-registry defines values for the code field in the channel-binding data and the channel-binding response, requires Standards Action for new registrations, allows early allocation, and has valid values from 0 to 255 with 0 reserved. The channel-binding namespaces sub-registry contains registrations for the NSID field, requires IETF Review, and also has valid values from 0 to 255 with 0 reserved.

A new sub-registry for EAP Lower Layers was created in the EAP Numbers registry. Registration requires Expert Review, and the expert's primary role is to prevent multiple registrations for the same lower layer. The initial registrations are 1 for wired IEEE 802.1X, 2 for IEEE 802.11 with no pre-authentication, 3 for IEEE 802.11 with pre-authentication, 4 for IEEE 802.16e, 5 for IKEv2, 6 for PPP, 7 for PANA with no pre-authentication, 8 for GSS-API, and 9 for PANA with pre-authentication. A new RADIUS attribute named EAP-Lower-Layer was registered with the value 163.
sections.plainLanguage: Two official lists were started, one for the message codes and one for the namespaces, plus a list naming the kinds of link EAP can run over. Nine link types were registered to begin with.

messages.label: Channel-binding response (code 2 or 3)

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: 1 for channel-binding data, 2 for a success response, 3 for a failure response.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Two octets in network byte order giving the length of the NS-Specific data; the NSID and length octets are not included.

fields.name: NSID
fields.desc: Namespace identifier; 1 is RADIUS and 255 is reserved for private use. The NS-Specific data follows.

items.label: Channel-binding data

items.label: Success
items.desc: The server confirms that the binding was validated.

items.label: Failure
items.desc: The server found the attributes did not describe the authenticator accurately.
